nodes.label: Binomial Theorem
nodes.note: The binomial theorem expands a power of a sum into a weighted sum of terms whose coefficients are binomial coefficients. The master formula is $$(a + b)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$ with general term $$T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$.

nodes.label: Expansion for Positive Integral Index
nodes.note: For a positive integer $$n$$ the expansion of $$(a + b)^n$$ has exactly $$n + 1$$ terms in which the powers of $$a$$ fall and the powers of $$b$$ rise, always summing to $$n$$. The compact form is $$(a + b)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$.

nodes.label: Theorem Statement and General Term
nodes.note: The theorem states $$(a + b)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$ and the $$(r+1)$$-th term from the beginning is $$T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$. The subscript $$r$$ is always one less than the term position, a detail that drives most indexing questions.

nodes.label: General Term
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_{r+1} = \binom{n}{r} a^{n-r} b^r$$, so to find the term containing a particular power one solves for $$r$$ from the exponent of $$a$$ or $$b$$. The coefficient of that term is the binomial coefficient $$\binom{n}{r}$$ times any numerical factors carried by $$a$$ and $$b$$.

nodes.label: Number of Terms and Homogeneity
nodes.note: The expansion of $$(a + b)^n$$ has exactly $$n + 1$$ terms, one more than the index, and in every term the exponents of $$a$$ and $$b$$ add up to $$n$$. This homogeneity $$(n - r) + r = n$$ is the quickest check that an expansion has been written correctly.

nodes.label: Canonical Form with Unity
nodes.note: Setting $$a = 1$$ and $$b = x$$ gives the canonical expansion $$(1 + x)^n = \sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} x^r = C_0 + C_1 x + C_2 x^2 + \dots + C_n x^n$$ where $$C_r = \binom{n}{r}$$. Almost every coefficient-series identity is derived from this single form by substituting values of $$x$$.

nodes.label: Middle Term Analytics
nodes.note: The location of the middle term depends on the parity of $$n$$: an even index gives one middle term and an odd index gives two. This is because the total number of terms $$n + 1$$ is odd for even $$n$$ and even for odd $$n$$.

nodes.label: Middle Term for Even Index
nodes.note: When $$n$$ is even there is a unique middle term, the $$\left(\frac{n}{2} + 1\right)$$-th term, equal to $$T_{\frac{n}{2} + 1} = \binom{n}{n/2} a^{n/2} b^{n/2}$$. Its coefficient $$\binom{n}{n/2}$$ is the largest binomial coefficient in the whole expansion.

nodes.label: Middle Terms for Odd Index
nodes.note: When $$n$$ is odd there are two middle terms, the $$\frac{n+1}{2}$$-th and the $$\frac{n+3}{2}$$-th, given by $$T_{\frac{n+1}{2}} = \binom{n}{\frac{n-1}{2}} a^{\frac{n+1}{2}} b^{\frac{n-1}{2}}$$ and $$T_{\frac{n+3}{2}} = \binom{n}{\frac{n+1}{2}} a^{\frac{n-1}{2}} b^{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$. The two coefficients $$\binom{n}{\frac{n-1}{2}}$$ and $$\binom{n}{\frac{n+1}{2}}$$ are equal and are the largest in the expansion.

nodes.label: Greatest Binomial Coefficient
nodes.note: The binomial coefficients rise to the middle and then fall symmetrically, so the greatest is $$\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2 \rfloor}$$. For even $$n$$ this is the single central coefficient and for odd $$n$$ the two central coefficients are equal and greatest.

nodes.label: Term from the End
nodes.note: The $$r$$-th term from the end of $$(a + b)^n$$ equals the $$r$$-th term from the beginning of $$(b + a)^n$$, that is $$T_r^{\text{end}} = T_{n-r+2}^{\text{beg}} = \binom{n}{r-1} a^{r-1} b^{n-r+1}$$. This reversal identity converts end-counting into the familiar beginning index.

nodes.label: Sum and Difference of Conjugate Expansions
nodes.note: Adding and subtracting the conjugate expansions gives $$(a + b)^n + (a - b)^n = 2\left[\binom{n}{0} a^n + \binom{n}{2} a^{n-2} b^2 + \dots\right]$$ and $$(a + b)^n - (a - b)^n = 2\left[\binom{n}{1} a^{n-1} b + \binom{n}{3} a^{n-3} b^3 + \dots\right]$$. The first isolates even-index terms and the second isolates odd-index terms.

nodes.label: Numerically Greatest Term
nodes.note: The numerically greatest term of $$(a + b)^n$$ for given numerical values of $$a$$ and $$b$$ is found by a ratio test on consecutive terms. It differs from the greatest binomial coefficient because it depends on the actual magnitudes of $$a$$ and $$b$$.

nodes.label: Ratio Test on Consecutive Terms
nodes.note: The ratio of consecutive terms is $$\left| \frac{T_{r+1}}{T_r} \right| = \frac{n - r + 1}{r} \left| \frac{b}{a} \right|$$, and the terms increase while this ratio is at least one. Solving the inequality $$(n - r + 1)|b| \ge r|a|$$ localizes the peak term.

nodes.label: The NGT Parameter m
nodes.note: The critical parameter is $$m = \frac{(n+1)|b|}{|a| + |b|} = \frac{n + 1}{1 + \left| \frac{a}{b} \right|}$$, and the terms increase up to $$r = m$$. Whether $$m$$ is an integer decides between two equal greatest terms and a single greatest term.

nodes.label: Integer m Gives Twin NGTs
nodes.note: When $$m$$ is an integer the ratio equals one at $$r = m$$, so $$|T_m| = |T_{m+1}|$$ and there are two numerically greatest terms, $$T_m$$ and $$T_{m+1}$$. The two terms have identical magnitude and both qualify as the NGT.

nodes.label: Non-Integer m Gives a Unique NGT
nodes.note: When $$m$$ is not an integer the terms increase strictly up to $$r = \lfloor m \rfloor$$ and decrease thereafter, giving a single numerically greatest term $$T_{\lfloor m \rfloor + 1}$$. The floor of $$m$$ therefore pins the unique peak term.

nodes.label: Greatest Coefficient versus NGT
nodes.note: The greatest binomial coefficient depends only on $$n$$ and always sits at the middle term, whereas the numerically greatest term depends on the values of $$a$$ and $$b$$ through $$m = \frac{(n+1)|b|}{|a| + |b|}$$. Confusing the two is the classic JEE trap: one is purely combinatorial and the other is numerical.

nodes.label: Binomial Coefficient Series
nodes.note: Substituting special values of $$x$$ into $$(1 + x)^n = \sum C_r x^r$$, and differentiating or integrating it, yields a family of coefficient identities. These are the standard tools for summing series built from $$C_r = \binom{n}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Sum of Coefficients
nodes.note: Setting $$x = 1$$ in the canonical expansion gives $$C_0 + C_1 + C_2 + \dots + C_n = 2^n$$, and setting $$x = -1$$ gives the alternating sum $$C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - \dots + (-1)^n C_n = 0$$. Adding and subtracting these two equations separates the even and odd indexed coefficients.

nodes.label: Even and Odd Indexed Sums
nodes.note: From the two substitutions one obtains $$C_0 + C_2 + C_4 + \dots = C_1 + C_3 + C_5 + \dots = 2^{n-1}$$, so the even-indexed and odd-indexed binomial coefficients each sum to half of $$2^n$$. This equal split is a favourite one-line JEE result.

nodes.label: Alternating Sum of Coefficients
nodes.note: The alternating sum $$C_0 - C_1 + C_2 - C_3 + \dots + (-1)^n C_n = 0$$ follows directly from substituting $$x = -1$$ into $$(1 + x)^n$$. It shows the positive and negative binomial coefficients cancel exactly for every positive index $$n$$.

nodes.label: Differentiation Method
nodes.note: Differentiating $$(1 + x)^n = \sum C_r x^r$$ with respect to $$x$$ and then setting $$x = 1$$ gives $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r \binom{n}{r} = n \cdot 2^{n-1}$$. The method works whenever the coefficient is multiplied by an arithmetic factor like $$r$$ or $$r^2$$.

nodes.label: Second Derivative Identity
nodes.note: Multiplying the first derivative by $$x$$ and differentiating again, then setting $$x = 1$$, gives $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^2 \binom{n}{r} = n(n+1) \cdot 2^{n-2}$$. The same double-differentiation trick extends to any polynomial weight in $$r$$.

nodes.label: Alternating Weighted Sum
nodes.note: Setting $$x = -1$$ after the first differentiation gives the alternating weighted sum $$\sum_{r=1}^{n} (-1)^{r-1} r \binom{n}{r} = 0$$ for $$n > 1$$. The cancellation reflects the fact that the linear function $$nx(1+x)^{n-1}$$ vanishes at $$x = -1$$.

nodes.label: Integration Method
nodes.note: Integrating $$(1 + x)^n = \sum C_r x^r$$ from $$0$$ to $$x$$ and setting $$x = 1$$ gives $$\sum_{r=0}^{n} \frac{\binom{n}{r}}{r+1} = \frac{2^{n+1} - 1}{n+1}$$. Integration is the dual of differentiation and handles coefficients divided by an arithmetic factor.

nodes.label: Product of Binomial Coefficients
nodes.note: Multiplying $$(1 + x)^n$$ by $$(x + 1)^n$$ and equating the coefficient of $$x^n$$ gives the sum of squares $$C_0^2 + C_1^2 + \dots + C_n^2 = \binom{2n}{n} = \frac{(2n)!}{(n!)^2}$$. Equating other coefficients yields the shifted convolution identities.

nodes.label: Shifted Convolution Products
nodes.note: Equating the coefficient of $$x^{n-k}$$ in the product $$(1+x)^n (x+1)^n = (1+x)^{2n}$$ gives $$\sum_{r=0}^{n-k} \binom{n}{r} \binom{n}{r+k} = \binom{2n}{n-k}$$. This convolution identity covers products of coefficients whose indices differ by a fixed shift $$k$$.

nodes.label: Pascal's Triangle Recursion
nodes.note: Each entry of Pascal's triangle is the sum of the two above it, expressed as $$\binom{n}{r} + \binom{n}{r-1} = \binom{n+1}{r}$$. The symmetry $$\binom{n}{r} = \binom{n}{n-r}$$ and the row sum $$\sum_{r=0}^{n} \binom{n}{r} = 2^n$$ are the other two structural facts.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Applications
nodes.note: The binomial theorem converts large powers into a multiple of a modulus plus a small remainder, which is the backbone of divisibility, remainder, and last-digit problems. The trick is to write the base as $$M \pm 1$$ or $$Mk \pm R$$ for the modulus $$M$$.

nodes.label: Divisibility and Remainders
nodes.note: To find the remainder of a large power $$A^n$$ on division by $$M$$, one writes $$A$$ (or a power of $$A$$) as $$kM \pm 1$$ and expands, since $$(M + 1)^n \equiv 1 \pmod{M}$$. All terms except the last are multiples of $$M$$ and drop out.

nodes.label: Remainder Example
nodes.note: To find the remainder when $$7^{103}$$ is divided by $$25$$, note $$7^2 = 49 = 2(25) - 1$$, so $$7^{103} = 7(50 - 1)^{51} = 7(50k - 1) = 350k - 7 = 25(14k - 1) + 18$$. The remainder is therefore $$18$$.

nodes.label: Proving Divisibility
nodes.note: To prove an expression like $$a^n - b^n$$ is divisible by $$a - b$$, one writes $$a = (a - b) + b$$ and expands $$[(a - b) + b]^n$$; every term except $$b^n$$ carries the factor $$(a - b)$$. The binomial expansion thus exhibits the divisor explicitly.

nodes.label: Last Digits Determination
nodes.note: The last digit of a number is its value modulo $$10$$, the last two digits are its value modulo $$100$$, and the last three are modulo $$1000$$. One expands the base as $$(10k \pm 1)^n$$ and retains only the terms that survive the chosen modulus.

nodes.label: Integral and Fractional Parts
nodes.note: For $$N = (A + \sqrt{B})^n = I + f$$ with $$A - 1 < \sqrt{B} < A$$, the conjugate bracket $$f' = (A - \sqrt{B})^n$$ lies strictly between $$0$$ and $$1$$. Adding the two brackets eliminates the surds and yields an even integer, forcing the fractional parts to sum to one.

nodes.label: The Conjugate Bracket
nodes.note: Defining $$f' = (A - \sqrt{B})^n$$ gives $$0 < f' < 1$$ because $$0 < |A - \sqrt{B}| < 1$$, and the sum $$(A + \sqrt{B})^n + (A - \sqrt{B})^n$$ is an even integer $$2K$$ since all odd surd powers cancel. As $$I + (f + f') = 2K$$ is an integer and $$0 < f + f' < 2$$, the fractional parts must satisfy $$f + f' = 1$$.

nodes.label: Integral Part Parity and Product
nodes.note: Because $$f + f' = 1$$ and the total is the even integer $$2K$$, the integral part is $$I = 2K - 1$$, always an odd integer. The product of the number and its conjugate is $$(I + f)(1 - f) = (I + f)f' = (A + \sqrt{B})^n (A - \sqrt{B})^n = (A^2 - B)^n$$, a clean rational value.

nodes.label: Binomial Theorem for Any Index
nodes.note: For a rational or negative index $$n$$ the expansion becomes an infinite series that converges only when the first term is unity and $$|x| < 1$$. The general term is $$T_{r+1} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!} x^r$$ and the series does not terminate.

nodes.label: Theorem for Rational Index
nodes.note: For any real $$n$$ the series $$(1 + x)^n = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^2 + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^3 + \dots$$ converges if and only if $$|x| < 1$$. The base must first be normalized so that the leading term is exactly $$1$$, since $$(a + x)^n = a^n\left(1 + \frac{x}{a}\right)^n$$ needs $$\left|\frac{x}{a}\right| < 1$$.

nodes.label: General Term for Any Index
nodes.note: The $$(r+1)$$-th term of the infinite series is $$T_{r+1} = \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots(n-r+1)}{r!} x^r$$, a ratio of $$r$$ falling factors of $$n$$ over $$r!$$. Unlike the positive-index case there are infinitely many terms, and convergence requires $$|x| < 1$$.

nodes.label: Square Root and Fractional Expansions
nodes.note: For a fractional index such as $$n = \frac{1}{2}$$ the series gives $$\sqrt{1 + x} = 1 + \frac{x}{2} - \frac{x^2}{8} + \frac{x^3}{16} - \dots$$ valid for $$|x| < 1$$. Such expansions are the source of many limit and approximation problems in JEE calculus.

nodes.label: Canonical Infinite Expansions
nodes.note: Four negative-power expansions recur constantly in JEE calculus and limits: $$(1 - x)^{-1}$$, $$(1 + x)^{-1}$$, $$(1 - x)^{-2}$$, and the general $$(1 - x)^{-n}$$. Each is an infinite series valid strictly for $$|x| < 1$$.

nodes.label: Expansion of (1 - x) to the -1
nodes.note: The geometric series is $$(1 - x)^{-1} = 1 + x + x^2 + x^3 + \dots = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} x^r$$ for $$|x| < 1$$, and its alternating twin is $$(1 + x)^{-1} = 1 - x + x^2 - x^3 + \dots = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (-1)^r x^r$$. Both diverge at $$x = 1$$.

nodes.label: Expansion of (1 - x) to the -2
nodes.note: Differentiating the geometric series gives $$(1 - x)^{-2} = 1 + 2x + 3x^2 + 4x^3 + \dots = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (r+1) x^r$$ for $$|x| < 1$$, with the alternating version $$(1 + x)^{-2} = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} (-1)^r (r+1) x^r$$. The coefficients are the natural numbers in arithmetic progression.

nodes.label: General Negative Power
nodes.note: The general negative integer power expands as $$(1 - x)^{-n} = \sum_{r=0}^{\infty} \binom{n+r-1}{r} x^r$$ for $$|x| < 1$$, so the coefficients are the diagonal binomial coefficients $$\binom{n+r-1}{r}$$. This unifies the $$-1$$ and $$-2$$ cases and connects to stars-and-bars counting.

nodes.label: Approximations for Small Quantities
nodes.note: When $$|x|$$ is very small the higher powers are negligible and $$(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$$, with a second-order correction $$(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2} x^2$$. These linear and quadratic approximations are used throughout JEE for estimation and limits.

nodes.label: Multinomial Theorem
nodes.note: The multinomial theorem generalizes the binomial to a sum of three or more terms raised to a power. The expansion of $$(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n$$ sums over all non-negative integer partitions of $$n$$ into $$k$$ parts.

nodes.label: Multinomial Expansion
nodes.note: The expansion is $$(x_1 + x_2 + \dots + x_k)^n = \sum \frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \cdots r_k!} x_1^{r_1} x_2^{r_2} \cdots x_k^{r_k}$$ summed over all $$r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_k = n$$. Each term is weighted by the multinomial coefficient and the exponents of the variables add up to $$n$$.

nodes.label: Multinomial Coefficient
nodes.note: The coefficient of the term $$x_1^{r_1} x_2^{r_2} \cdots x_k^{r_k}$$ is the multinomial coefficient $$\frac{n!}{r_1! r_2! \cdots r_k!}$$, which counts the ways to partition $$n$$ objects into groups of sizes $$r_1, r_2, \dots, r_k$$. For $$k = 2$$ it reduces to the ordinary binomial coefficient $$\binom{n}{r}$$.

nodes.label: Total Number of Terms
nodes.note: Each distinct term corresponds to a non-negative integer solution of $$r_1 + r_2 + \dots + r_k = n$$, so by stars and bars the total number of terms is $$\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$$. This count depends only on $$n$$ and $$k$$, not on the variables themselves.

nodes.label: Trinomial Expansion
nodes.note: For three terms the number of distinct terms in $$(x + y + z)^n$$ is $$\binom{n+2}{2} = \frac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}$$, obtained by setting $$k = 3$$ in the general count $$\binom{n+k-1}{k-1}$$. Before applying this one must simplify the base, since a perfect-square base collapses the effective number of terms.

nodes.label: Greatest Multinomial Coefficient
nodes.note: The multinomial coefficient is maximized when the indices $$r_1, r_2, \dots, r_k$$ are as nearly equal as possible, i.e. as close to $$n/k$$ as integer partitions allow. Writing $$n = qk + r$$ with $$q = \lfloor n/k \rfloor$$, the maximum is $$\frac{n!}{(q!)^{k-r}\,[(q+1)!]^r}$$ with $$r$$ indices equal to $$q + 1$$ and the rest equal to $$q$$.

nodes.label: Term-Counting Caution
nodes.note: A base that is secretly a perfect power must be condensed first: $$(1 + 2x + x^2)^{20} = [(1 + x)^2]^{20} = (1 + x)^{40}$$ has exactly $$40 + 1 = 41$$ dissimilar terms, not the $$\binom{22}{2} = 231$$ that a blind trinomial count would give. Always simplify the polynomial base before applying any term-counting formula.
